name: The Utility Monster
statement: If one being gained far more happiness from each resource than anyone else, strict utilitarianism would tell everyone to feed it everything.
statementAccent: would tell everyone to feed it everything
meaning: The utility monster is a thought experiment introduced by the philosopher Robert Nozick in his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia as an objection to utilitarianism, the view that the right action is the one that maximises total utility or well-being. Nozick imagines a being, the utility monster, who is far more efficient than anyone else at converting resources into happiness or utility, gaining enormously more satisfaction from each unit of resource than an ordinary person loses by giving it up. A utilitarianism that seeks to maximise total utility would then be committed to funnelling nearly all resources to the monster, since doing so yields the greatest total sum, even if this leaves everyone else destitute. Nozick argues that this conclusion is monstrous and counterintuitive, revealing a flaw in the idea that maximising aggregate utility is all that matters, and showing that simple utilitarian aggregation can sacrifice the many for the one.
mechanism: The argument exploits the aggregative structure of utilitarianism. If rightness is fixed by the total sum of utility, then how utility is distributed across people does not matter in itself; only the sum does. Introduce a being whose capacity to gain utility from resources vastly exceeds everyone else's, so that transferring a resource from an ordinary person to the monster always increases the total. A theory that maximises the sum must then keep transferring until nearly everything goes to the monster, however impoverished this leaves the rest. The result is a reductio: a supposedly benevolent principle demands that most people be sacrificed to feed one insatiable being. This exposes utilitarianism's neglect of distribution and of the separateness of persons, the idea that individuals are distinct and cannot simply have their losses cancelled by another's larger gains, which is central to Nozick's and John Rawls's critiques of aggregation.

examples.text: Because the monster gains more happiness from each resource than others lose, summing utility tells everyone to hand over their resources to it, ending in mass sacrifice.
The case dramatizes the objection that utilitarian aggregation ignores that people are distinct, treating one being's huge gains as offsetting many others' losses.
Debates about whether a future artificial mind able to experience vast pleasure should command resources revive the utility-monster worry in a new setting.

variants.name: The distribution objection
variants.text: The general complaint that maximising total utility is indifferent to how well-being is spread, allowing gross inequality if it raises the sum.

variants.name: The separateness of persons
variants.text: The deeper principle the monster illustrates, that individuals are distinct and one person's gains cannot simply compensate another's losses.

whyItMatters: The utility monster is a classic objection in moral philosophy, a vivid challenge to utilitarianism and to any purely aggregative theory of the good. It shows that maximising the total sum of welfare can license grotesque results, sacrificing the many to satisfy one, and thereby presses the case that distribution and the separateness of persons matter morally, not just the total. The argument has shaped debates over how to weigh utilities across people, motivating alternatives such as prioritarian and egalitarian views that give extra weight to the worse off, and it recurs in contemporary discussions of population ethics and of hypothetical minds with vast capacities for welfare.

working.text: imagine a monster that turns each resource into far more utility than anyone else would gain or lose, so giving it resources always raises the total.
let a utilitarianism that maximises the sum follow its logic, which directs nearly all resources to the monster whatever the cost to others.
treat the monstrous result, mass sacrifice to feed one being, as evidence that maximising aggregate utility cannot be the whole of morality.

limits: The utility monster is a counterexample aimed at simple aggregative utilitarianism; how decisive it is depends on the version targeted, and utilitarians have offered replies, questioning whether such unbounded utility is coherent or possible, or adopting views that discount the very rich in utility. Variants of consequentialism that build in equality, priority to the worse off, or diminishing marginal weight can blunt the objection. The scenario is also an idealisation, positing a being whose capacity for welfare has no natural ceiling, which some argue is not a genuine possibility. So the experiment functions as a serious challenge to one family of theories rather than a refutation of consequentialism in general, and responses to it are part of an ongoing debate.
misreadings: The monster is an objection to maximising total utility, not a claim that helping the happiest person is always wrong; it targets indifference to distribution, not benevolence as such. It does not refute all consequentialism, since theories that weight equality or priority to the worse off can resist it, so citing it as sinking utilitarianism wholesale overstates the case. And the point is not that the monster is realistic but that the principle of pure aggregation licenses its demands even in principle, which is what reveals the flaw the experiment is designed to expose.
origin: Introduced by the philosopher Robert Nozick in his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia as an objection to utilitarian aggregation, arguing that maximising total utility could require sacrificing everyone to a being that gains disproportionate utility from resources.
